title: Why Do Stock Markets Suddenly Crash? The Nasdaq's Worst Week Since 2020, Explained
fb_caption: In the week to 20 November 2026, the Nasdaq fell about 10%, its worst week since 2020, as a selloff in AI and chip stocks spread from Wall Street to Tokyo. So why do markets climb slowly but fall so fast? Here are the three big reasons: bubbles, fear and forced selling, plus what history says. Educational only, not financial advice. Did last week's drop worry you? Tell us below.

beats.text: Last week, the Nasdaq had its worst week since 2020. It fell about ten percent in five days, as a selloff in AI and chip stocks spread from Wall Street all the way to Tokyo.
So how can so much money vanish in just a few days? Because markets usually climb by the stairs, but fall by the elevator.
Here are the three big reasons. One: expectations. When everyone gets excited about a new technology, prices can run far ahead of real profits. People call that a bubble.
And a bubble doesn't need a big shock to pop. Sometimes one piece of bad news makes investors stop and ask: is this really worth the price?
Two: fear spreads. When prices start falling, many investors sell simply because everyone else is selling. Nobody wants to be the last one out the door.
Three: forced selling. Some investors buy stocks with borrowed money. When prices drop, lenders can demand cash back, and automatic sell orders kick in. Selling triggers more selling, like dominoes.
It's happened before. In 1987, US stocks fell more than twenty percent in a single day. In 2020, they crashed in a few weeks, then recovered within months.
